SteerDistill: Quantizing LLM Agents via Closed-Loop Teacher Steering

Genming Cui∗,†*,\dagger Affiliation: Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR), Tsinghua University Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China    Xiangyu Li∗,‡*,\ddagger Affiliation: Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR), Tsinghua University    Zixu Hao Affiliation: Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR), Tsinghua University    Xin Ding†\dagger Affiliation: Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR), Tsinghua University Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China    Yunxin Liu Affiliation: Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR), Tsinghua University    Ting Cao§\lx@sectionsign Affiliation: Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR), Tsinghua University
2026-11-07
Abstract

Low-bit quantization reduces the inference cost of LLM agents but can compromise task success. Examining failed rollouts, we find that quantized agents overlook task requirements or environmental conditions, producing environment transitions that diverge from successful full-precision references. Correcting these behavioral divergences remains difficult: offline data may miss the student’s failure contexts, while its own rollouts may provide few correct responses in those contexts. We introduce SteerDistill, a quantization-aware distillation method in which a full-precision teacher guides the student to revise failed responses and iteratively refines its guidance using feedback from student execution. This closed-loop teacher steering produces locally verified behavioral corrections. We internalize these corrections by training the student without guidance to match the steered student’s predictions at corrected turns and the full-precision teacher’s at other turns, enabling unassisted inference. Across five agentic benchmarks and three models, SteerDistill exceeds the strongest quantized baseline by 1.67–2.18 points in average score under W4A16 and stays within one point of BF16. On τ2\tau^{2}-Bench, it outperforms QeRL by 1.84 percentage points in success rate using 67% fewer training GPU hours and produces shorter successful trajectories than the quantized baselines.

1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents call tools and interact with their environments over multiple turns to complete tasks [52, 49, 42, 47, 24]. Repeated model calls make inference cost a central deployment concern [40, 54, 22], and low-bit quantization offers a practical way to reduce it [9, 44, 23, 21, 14, 7]. However, quantized agents often fall short of their full-precision counterparts in task success.

Examining failed rollouts, we find that quantized agents overlook task requirements or environmental conditions, producing environment transitions that differ from those of successful full-precision references (Sections D.1 and D.2). We refer to this mismatch as behavioral divergence. For example, an agent tries to read a file before entering its directory, although the available reading tool only accesses files in the current directory (Figures 1 and 11). In another task, an agent creates the requested files but leaves some empty instead of writing the specified contents (Figure 6).

However, identifying and correcting these behavioral divergences remain challenging. Offline training and distillation [5, 19, 8, 46] rely on data collected independently of the student’s interactions and may therefore miss the contexts in which it diverges. On-policy rollouts [13, 30, 1] address this coverage gap, but may provide few correct responses in those contexts. In our BFCL V4 multi-turn diagnostic, the student’s unguided retries yield a correct action at only 9.6% of divergent turns.11 1 We report turn-level Pass@4, the fraction of selected turns with at least one correct action in four attempts. Each attempt starts from the same pre-turn history and environment state.

Contribution.

We introduce SteerDistill, a quantization-aware distillation (QAD) method for LLM agents (Figure 1). The key idea is to construct and internalize teacher-guided behavioral corrections. During training, a full-precision teacher identifies the task requirements and environmental conditions overlooked by the student and provides targeted guidance for choosing an appropriate action. The student generates and executes a revised response, and the teacher refines its guidance using execution feedback. We call this process closed-loop teacher steering. By distilling these teacher-guided behavioral corrections, we train the student to take appropriate actions without teacher guidance at inference.

Two designs implement this approach. (i) Teacher-steered trajectory revision constructs behavioral corrections by revising failed student rollouts through closed-loop teacher steering. We use successful teacher references to locate behavioral divergences. At each divergence, the student revises its response from the restored pre-error context, and locally verified corrections are retained for distillation. In the same diagnostic, teacher steering raises turn-level Pass@4 from 9.6% to 82.3%. (ii) Internalization of steered behavior distills the locally verified corrections while retaining full-precision teacher supervision at other turns. At corrected turns, the student learns from the frozen steered student’s predictions without receiving the guidance.

Without teacher guidance at inference, SteerDistill achieves the strongest quantized performance in our comparisons, with lower training cost and shorter successful trajectories. (i) Accuracy. Across five agentic benchmarks and three models under W4A1622 2 WxxAyy denotes xx-bit weights and yy-bit activations., it exceeds the strongest quantized baseline by 1.67–2.18 points in average score and stays within one point of BF16; on Qwen3-8B under W2A16, the margin grows to 3.39 points (Table 1). (ii) Training cost. On τ2\tau^{2}-Bench, SteerDistill outperforms QeRL by 1.84 percentage points in success rate using 67% fewer training GPU hours (Figure 3). (iii) Inference cost. On τ2\tau^{2}-Bench, its successful tasks use 4.0K output tokens on average, close to BF16’s 3.9K, versus 4.1K–5.2K for the quantized baselines (Figure 3). (iv) Design insights. Ablations support intervening at behavioral divergences, guiding the student to generate its own corrections, retaining locally verified corrections, and using different distillation objectives at corrected and other turns (Table 2).

2 Related work

Capability recovery for low-bit LLM quantization.

To preserve model capabilities under low-bit quantization, one line of work improves the fidelity of quantized representations through weight reconstruction, scaling, and rotation [9, 23, 44, 35, 2, 25]. Complementary training-based approaches recover task performance using hard token targets [5, 19], soft distributions from full-precision teachers [8, 46, 30], or verifiable rewards [13, 30]. For quantized LLM agents, however, the available training data (including offline data and on-policy rollouts) may lack effective corrections in contexts where the student overlooks task requirements or environmental conditions. To address this, we extend quantization-aware distillation with closed-loop teacher steering to construct and internalize behavioral corrections (Sections 3.1 and 3.2).

Teacher guidance and context distillation for LLM agents.

Teacher-generated responses [39, 20, 26] and rollouts conditioned on privileged context [18, 45] give students access to improved training trajectories. To assess the value of such assistance, FutureBridge-OPD [4] evaluates teacher interventions through the distillation signals in subsequent student rollouts. OVCSD [43] instead uses task success to verify privileged continuations from student failure states, providing outcome-grounded corrective supervision. Our closed-loop teacher steering instead evaluates student corrections at the divergent turn, checking their environment transitions against the successful reference and using feedback from failed attempts to refine guidance. For quantized agents, this local loop targets overlooked task requirements and environmental conditions. We internalize these corrections through context distillation, following prior work on transferring the benefits of privileged information to unguided learners [53, 11].

3 Method

SteerDistill constructs and internalizes behavioral corrections in each training cycle (Figure 2). Teacher-steered trajectory revision (Section 3.1) revises the current student’s failed rollouts through closed-loop teacher steering and retains locally verified corrections. Internalization of steered behavior (Section 3.2) then trains the student on the retained trajectories without guidance, learning from the steered student at corrected turns and the full-precision teacher at other turns. The updated student generates the next batch of rollouts.

Setup.

Let πT\pi_{T} be the frozen full-precision teacher and πθ≡πQ⁡(θ)\pi_{\theta}\equiv\pi_{Q(\theta)} the trainable quantized student initialized from the same checkpoint, where θ\theta denotes the master weights and QQ is a fixed quantization operator. At turn tt, the student generates a response yty_{t} given history hth_{t}, comprising the task, previous responses, and environment observations. A response may include reasoning followed by an action or answer. During cycle kk, a frozen snapshot πθk\pi_{\theta_{k}} generates the initial rollouts and steered revisions. Distillation updates the learner πθ\pi_{\theta} on the retained trajectories to obtain θk+1\theta_{k+1} for the next cycle.

3.1 Teacher-steered trajectory revision

For each failed student rollout, we seek a successful teacher reference for the same task and initial environment state. This reference remains fixed throughout revision. Successful student rollouts and failed rollouts without a successful reference are retained unchanged for distillation.

Localizing an intervention turn.

We align the student and reference trajectories by their environment transitions, using only environment states to determine a match. Actions that produce matching transitions are treated as equivalent. We intervene at the first behavioral divergence, denoting the student turn by t⋆t^{\star} (Table 2, Q1). To revise this decision in its original context, we restore the history and environment state before t⋆t^{\star}.

Closed-loop teacher steering.

The teacher uses the failed response and successful reference to identify task requirements or environmental conditions overlooked by the student (Figure 2, i). It provides a steering prompt Gt⋆G_{t^{\star}} that explains the discrepancy, the conditions under which the guidance applies, and a corrective rule (Table 2, Q3). Conditioned on Gt⋆G_{t^{\star}}, the frozen student generates a revised response yt⋆∼πθk(⋅∣ht⋆,Gt⋆)y_{t^{\star}}\sim\pi_{\theta_{k}}(\cdot\mid h_{t^{\star}},G_{t^{\star}}) and executes its action.

We then locally verify the revised response by comparing the resulting environment states and returned information with those of the reference. If verification fails, the teacher refines its guidance using feedback from the attempt, and the student retries from the same pre-error history and state. The loop continues until a correction is locally verified or the per-turn attempt budget is exhausted. We compare teacher steering with unguided retries and teacher takeover in Table 2 (Q2).

Retaining verified corrections.

Once a revised response passes local verification, we retain it and its steering prompt for distillation. The response replaces the failed turn, and the student generates a new continuation without guidance. If the task still fails, we realign the revised rollout with the fixed reference to locate the next behavioral divergence. Revision stops when the task succeeds, no further divergence can be located, or an intervention exhausts its attempt budget. The current trajectory and its verified corrections are retained for distillation even if the task remains unsolved. Table 2 (Q4) evaluates both local verification and retaining corrections without requiring terminal success. Algorithm 1 and implementation details appear in Appendix A.

3.2 Internalization of steered behavior

We train the student on the retained trajectories using two sources of supervision: the steered student at corrected turns and the full-precision teacher at all other turns (Figure 2, ii). The learner receives no steering prompts in either case. Following prior work on turn-specific distillation [20], we use forward KL at corrected turns and reverse KL elsewhere (Table 2, Q5).

Learning from the steered student.

At a corrected turn, we retrieve the steering prompt GG that elicited the accepted response. Let cc denote the interaction history and the prefix of that response, with all steering prompts removed. The frozen student snapshot πθk\pi_{\theta_{k}} predicts each token from (c,G)(c,G), while the learner πθ\pi_{\theta} predicts from cc alone. We minimize forward KL to match the steered student’s predictions:

ℓFKL(c,G;θ)=DKL(πθk(⋅∣c,G)∥πθ(⋅∣c)).\ell_{\mathrm{FKL}}(c,G;\theta)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta_{k}}(\cdot\mid c,G)\,\middle\|\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid c)\right). (1)

Retaining teacher supervision.

At all other turns, including continuation turns that receive no further correction, we retain full-precision teacher supervision on the student-generated responses [1]. The teacher and learner receive the same context cc without guidance. We minimize reverse KL:

ℓRKL(c;θ)=DKL(πθ(⋅∣c)∥πT(⋅∣c)).\ell_{\mathrm{RKL}}(c;\theta)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid c)\,\middle\|\,\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid c)\right). (2)

Training objective.

We assign the loss by turn and average over all retained assistant-response tokens. For trajectory ii, let ℐi\mathcal{I}_{i} denote its retained corrected turns, each with its steering prompt Gi,tG_{i,t}. For turn tt and token jj, write ci,t,j=(hi,t,yi,t,<j)c_{i,t,j}=(h_{i,t},y_{i,t,<j}). Let 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k} contain all retained assistant-token positions (i,t,j)(i,t,j) in cycle kk. The objective is

ℒ(k)​(θ)=1|𝒜k|​∑(i,t,j)∈𝒜k{ℓFKL​(ci,t,j,Gi,t,θ),t∈ℐi,ℓRKL​(ci,t,j,θ),t∉ℐi.\mathcal{L}^{(k)}(\theta)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}_{k}|}\sum_{(i,t,j)\in\mathcal{A}_{k}}\begin{cases}\ell_{\mathrm{FKL}}(c_{i,t,j},G_{i,t};\theta),&t\in\mathcal{I}_{i},\\[2.0pt] \ell_{\mathrm{RKL}}(c_{i,t,j};\theta),&t\notin\mathcal{I}_{i}.\end{cases} (3)

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental setup

Benchmarks and metrics.

We evaluate on five agentic benchmarks: BFCL V4 [32], τ2\tau^{2}-Bench [3], WebShop [51], ALFWorld [37], and Search QA. We report the official Overall score for BFCL V4. For τ2\tau^{2}-Bench, we report success rate (Pass@1) in the main table and Pass@4 in Section C.2. We likewise report success rate (SR) for WebShop and ALFWorld and include WebShop Task Score in the appendix. For Search QA, we follow Search-R1 [15] and compute Exact Match (EM) scores on seven question-answering datasets.33 3 Natural Questions (NQ) [17], TriviaQA [16], PopQA [28], HotpotQA [50], 2WikiMultiHopQA [12], MuSiQue [38], and Bamboogle [33]. We report their unweighted mean in the main table and per-dataset EM in the appendix.

Models and training data.

We evaluate SteerDistill and the baselines on three models: Qwen3-8B [48], Qwen3.5-4B [34], and Gemma 4 12B-it [10]. For each model, we obtain task-specific BF16 checkpoints through GRPO post-training [36].44 4 GRPO post-training provides a stronger starting checkpoint for both the teacher and the quantized student. We also report results starting directly from the original Qwen3-8B backbone in Section C.1. Each checkpoint serves as the full-precision reference and frozen teacher, and initializes all quantized methods. We use the same task-specific data or environments for BF16 post-training and subsequent low-bit training.

For BFCL V4 and τ2\tau^{2}-Bench, we train on executable tool-use tasks from AgentWorldModel [41] and evaluate the same tool-use checkpoint on both benchmarks. For WebShop and ALFWorld, we use their respective training environments. For Search QA, we follow Search-R1 [15] and use the training sets of NQ [17] and HotpotQA [50]. We evaluate on all seven datasets, treating NQ and HotpotQA as in-domain and the remaining five as out-of-domain.

Baselines.

We compare with five baselines for quantization and capability recovery: (i) GPTQ [9] for post-training quantization (PTQ); (ii) EfficientQAT [5] for quantization-aware training (QAT); (iii) BitDistiller [8] for offline quantization-aware distillation (QAD); (iv) On-Policy QAD, implemented following NVIDIA NeMo-RL’s quantization-aware distillation workflow [29]; and (v) QeRL [13] for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.55 5 The reference configurations for NeMo-RL’s QAD workflow and QeRL use NVFP4 on Hopper or Blackwell GPUs. We adapt both workflows to our group-wise integer quantization setup on A100 GPUs. All training-based methods converge within the two-epoch training budget. Detailed training settings appear in Appendix B.

Quantization and evaluation protocol.

We evaluate all three models with INT4 weights and BF16 activations (W4A16). For Qwen3-8B, we additionally evaluate INT4 weights with INT8 activations (W4A8) and INT2 weights with BF16 activations (W2A16). At inference, SteerDistill uses only the trained quantized student, without the teacher or steering prompts.

4.2 Main results

Gains across all five benchmarks.

On Qwen3-8B under W4A16, SteerDistill outperforms all quantized baselines on each of the five benchmarks (Table 1). Its average score of 53.18 exceeds the strongest baseline, QeRL, by 2.18 points. With a remaining gap of only 0.36 points to the BF16 reference, SteerDistill recovers nearly all of the performance lost to quantization.

Near-BF16 performance across models.

On Qwen3.5-4B and Gemma 4 12B-it under the same W4A16 setting, SteerDistill improves the average score over the strongest quantized baseline, QeRL, by 1.71 and 1.67 points, respectively. Across all three models, its average score remains within one point of the corresponding BF16 reference.

Gains persist at lower precisions.

On Qwen3-8B, SteerDistill retains the highest average score under both W4A8 and W2A16. It outperforms the strongest quantized baseline in each setting: QeRL by 1.93 points under W4A8 and On-Policy QAD by 3.39 points under W2A16. Across these two settings, it also outperforms the quantized baselines on every benchmark except Search QA under W2A16, where BitDistiller scores 34.22 versus 34.05 for SteerDistill.

4.3 Efficiency

Higher success rates with less training.

On Qwen3-8B, SteerDistill achieves higher Pass@1 on τ2\tau^{2}-Bench with fewer GPU hours than On-Policy QAD and QeRL (Figure 3). Its intermediate checkpoint at 32 GPU hours reaches 31.68%, exceeding On-Policy QAD’s converged score at about 40 GPU hours by 2.91 percentage points. It also outperforms QeRL at 96 GPU hours by 1.84 percentage points while using 67% fewer GPU hours. This faster recovery is consistent with the targeted supervision provided by locally verified behavioral corrections.

Higher success rates with fewer output tokens.

On Qwen3-8B under W4A16, SteerDistill achieves higher Pass@1 on τ2\tau^{2}-Bench with fewer output tokens per successful task than the quantized baselines (Figure 3). Averaging over each method’s own successful tasks, we obtain 4.0K output tokens for SteerDistill, compared with 4.1K–5.2K for the quantized baselines and 3.9K for BF16. Its successful trajectories also involve fewer interaction steps and tool calls than those of the quantized baselines (Table 7). The W4A8 and W2A16 results show the same pattern (Section C.3).

4.4 Ablation studies and analysis

We examine the design choices for constructing and internalizing behavioral corrections on BFCL V4 using Qwen3-8B under W4A16 (Table 2). Q1–Q4 examine correction construction: where to intervene, how to generate corrections, and how to verify and retain them. Q5 then tests the distillation objectives used for internalization at corrected and other turns. All scores discussed below are BFCL V4 Overall scores.

Q1 (Intervention localization): Intervene at the behavioral divergence, not action mismatch.

We use environment states to intervene at the first behavioral divergence rather than the first action mismatch. This improves the score by 1.83 points. Different actions can produce the same environment transition, so intervening on action mismatches can introduce unnecessary revisions into the distillation data. Intervening at a random eligible turn yields 43.52, even below On-Policy QAD’s 44.43.

Q2 (Intervention strategy): Steer the student instead of directly taking over.

From the same restored history and environment state, we compare student retry without guidance, direct response replacement by the teacher, and student revision under teacher guidance. The student continues the rollout in all three cases. Steering improves the score by 2.38 points over retry and 1.78 points over takeover.

Q3 (Steering format and source): Use structured steering prompts generated by the teacher.

We compare two formats for the teacher’s steering prompts: structured prompts that separately state the discrepancy, applicable conditions, and corrective rule, and free-form prompts without a prescribed structure. With the intervention turn, reference, and verification fixed, the structured format gains 2.06 points. This result is consistent with prior findings on the benefits of specific, actionable feedback and feedback organized around explicit requirements [27, 6]. Keeping the structured format and reference fixed, we obtain gains of 5.10 points over the student and 1.57 points over GPT-5.6-Sol [31] by using the full-precision teacher as the prompt source. Section D.3 compares the resulting prompts and student continuations in a ticket-creation task.

Q4 (Revision retention): Retain locally verified corrections even when the task fails.

Removing local verification substantially lowers the score from 46.84 to 42.18. Once corrections are locally verified, additionally requiring terminal task success yields a slightly lower score of 46.30. This filter discards verified corrections from unsuccessful trajectories without improving performance.

Q5 (Distillation routing): Use forward KL at corrected turns and reverse KL elsewhere.

We keep the retained trajectories, target models, and input contexts fixed and vary only the KL direction. Using forward KL (FKL) at corrected turns and reverse KL (RKL) elsewhere gains 1.55 points over RKL throughout and 2.26 points over FKL throughout. Reversing this assignment lowers the score by 2.56 points.

5 Conclusion

SteerDistill recovers the agentic capabilities of quantized LLMs through closed-loop teacher steering and distillation. By targeting the task requirements and environmental conditions overlooked at behavioral divergences, the teacher guides the student to generate its own corrections and refines its guidance using execution feedback. Distillation internalizes the locally verified behavioral corrections for unassisted inference. Across five benchmarks and three models, SteerDistill improves over quantized baselines under W4A16 and stays within one point of BF16 in average score. On τ2\tau^{2}-Bench, it outperforms QeRL by 1.84 percentage points in success rate using 67% fewer training GPU hours and produces shorter successful trajectories than the quantized baselines. We discuss limitations in Appendix E.

Appendix A Implementation details of SteerDistill

We provide implementation details for trajectory revision and distillation, following the two stages in Section 3. Table 3 summarizes the notation.

A.1 Teacher-steered trajectory revision

Algorithm 1 specifies how a student rollout is revised and retained for distillation.

Environment states and alignment.

We align student and reference trajectories using environment states to match their transitions. In AgentWorldModel, state is represented by task-relevant database contents. ALFWorld uses world facts and available actions. WebShop uses product selections, page type, and available choices. Search QA uses retrieved evidence as its information state.

Matching state transitions can result from different actions and occur at different turn indices. We select the first divergent student turn t⋆t^{\star} for intervention and use the corresponding reference transition ρT\rho^{T} to verify candidate revisions.

Local verification.

Local verification determines whether a candidate response can replace the divergent turn. In AgentWorldModel, we require the database states before and after execution to match those of the reference and reject responses that cause environment errors. Read operations must also return matching information. For a terminal response, we require the reference to terminate as well and the candidate to pass the task verifier.

In ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search QA, we accept a valid candidate if its resulting environment state matches the reference or if both executions achieve task success. This allows successful executions to end in different states. Verification returns an acceptance flag vv and a report ff with the result and, on rejection, the failure category used to refine steering.

Steering prompts and feedback.

The teacher forms a steering prompt GG from the aligned discrepancy and memory ℳ\mathcal{M}. This memory stores the latest accepted steering prompt within the current trajectory, allowing the teacher to incorporate earlier guidance that remains applicable. The new prompt explains the discrepancy, the conditions under which its corrective rule applies, the expected transition, and how to verify it.

We allow up to RR attempts at each intervention. Before each attempt, we restore the same pre-error history and environment state. The frozen student then generates a response conditioned on GG and executes its action. If local verification rejects the attempt, we append its prompt, candidate assistant content and tool calls, termination status, and verification report ff to the feedback history FF. The teacher uses summaries of FF, together with the original failed rollout, fixed reference, and memory ℳ\mathcal{M}, to refine GG for another attempt. Feedback history FF is reset at each new intervention, while memory ℳ\mathcal{M} carries accepted guidance across interventions.

Continuation and retained data.

Once a response passes local verification, it replaces the response at t⋆t^{\star}, and the old suffix is discarded. We remove correction records at or after t⋆t^{\star} from ℐ\mathcal{I} and 𝒢\mathcal{G}, then record the corrected turn in ℐ\mathcal{I} and its steering prompt in 𝒢\mathcal{G}. This prompt also becomes the new memory ℳ\mathcal{M}. From the resulting environment state and observation, the student generates a new continuation without guidance. If the task still fails, we realign the revised trajectory with the fixed reference to locate the next behavioral divergence.

Revision stops when the task succeeds, all RR attempts at an intervention fail local verification, or no further divergence can be aligned with the reference. In all cases, we retain the current trajectory together with ℐ\mathcal{I} and 𝒢\mathcal{G} for distillation, including accepted corrections in trajectories that remain unsuccessful. If no correction was accepted, we retain the original student rollout.

A.2 Internalization of steered behavior

The retained trajectories provide the histories and response tokens used for distillation. At turns in ℐ\mathcal{I}, we use the corresponding prompts in 𝒢\mathcal{G} to compute targets from the steered student. At all other turns, targets come from the full-precision teacher. The learner receives no steering prompts in either case.

Quantized generation and optimization.

The teacher and student start from the same BF16 checkpoint. The teacher stays frozen, while the student maintains trainable BF16 master weights. In cycle kk, we use a frozen snapshot θk\theta_{k} in the low-bit runtime for rollout generation and revision.

During distillation, we recompute the FKL target πθk(⋅∣c,G)\pi_{\theta_{k}}(\cdot\mid c,G) at corrected turns using a frozen fake-quantized copy of the same snapshot and the stored steering prompt GG. At all other turns, the full-precision teacher supplies the RKL target πT(⋅∣c)\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid c). For both targets, cc is the same retained history and response prefix used by the learner.

The learner πθ(⋅∣c)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid c) uses fake quantization in its forward pass, with gradients propagated to its BF16 master weights through the straight-through estimator. The updated master weights form snapshot θk+1\theta_{k+1}, which is quantized for rollout generation and revision in the next cycle.

Loss computation and masking.

For each retained assistant turn, we compute loss only on its response tokens. These include assistant text and serialized tool calls, as well as reasoning and termination tokens when present. System and user messages, environment observations, and steering prompts are excluded from the loss. Discarded responses and suffixes are excluded from training.

We reuse the token IDs recorded during generation when available. Otherwise, we tokenize the retained response and append an EOS token unless generation was truncated by length.

At each supervised response-token position, we compute KL over the full vocabulary, using FKL for corrected turns and RKL for all other turns. This assignment also applies to regenerated continuations. The objective in Equation 3 averages over all supervised response tokens, so corrected and other turns are weighted by their respective token counts.

Appendix B Evaluation details

Training settings.

Table 4 lists the hyperparameters used for the low-bit training stage. All training-based methods use the same learning rate, trajectory batch size, and total number of epochs. EfficientQAT divides its two epochs evenly between Block-AP and E2E-QP. All training-based methods converge within this two-epoch budget.

The methods retain their respective optimization settings. BitDistiller uses AdamW with a constant learning rate and zero weight decay. On-Policy QAD follows NVIDIA NeMo-RL’s quantization-aware distillation workflow, using a rollout temperature of 1.0 and top-64 teacher logits. QeRL uses GRPO with temperature 1.0 and clipping bounds (0.2,0.28)(0.2,0.28), together with AdamW-8bit and its official adaptive quantization-noise configuration. For SteerDistill, we set the attempt budget to R=4R=4 at each intervention in teacher-steered trajectory revision (Appendix A).

For SteerDistill, we follow the asymmetric group-wise quantization implementation in BitDistiller [8], including its calibration and clipping settings. We use a weight group size of 64 across all quantized methods. All experiments run on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs.

Inference settings.

We follow the benchmark evaluation protocols and use the same inference settings for all quantized methods within each benchmark. We use temperatures of 0.001 for BFCL V4, 0 for τ2\tau^{2}-Bench, and 0.7 for WebShop, ALFWorld, and Search QA. Each response is limited to 32,768 output tokens, except in WebShop and ALFWorld, where the limit is 4,096. Interaction limits are 200 steps for τ2\tau^{2}-Bench, 15 for WebShop, 50 for ALFWorld, and 4 for Search QA; BFCL V4 follows the official evaluator’s limits. The τ2\tau^{2}-Bench user simulator uses GPT-5.6 at temperature 0. For Search QA, we retrieve three passages per query.

Appendix C Additional results

C.1 Results without initial GRPO

We initialize SteerDistill and three quantized baselines directly from the original Qwen3-8B checkpoint, without initial task-specific GRPO post-training. This checkpoint also serves as the BF16 reference and frozen teacher. Apart from the initial checkpoint, all training settings match the main Qwen3-8B W4A16 experiments (Sections 4.1 and 4).

Table 5 shows that SteerDistill outperforms the three quantized baselines on both benchmarks and remains within one point of BF16. All methods score lower than their post-GRPO counterparts in Table 1, while their relative ordering remains unchanged.

C.2 Additional evaluation metrics

Table 6 supplements the main results for Qwen3-8B under W4A16. For τ2\tau^{2}-Bench, we supplement Pass@1 with Pass@4, the fraction of tasks solved at least once in four runs. WebShop Task Score complements the success rate by measuring how well the selected product satisfies the user’s requirements. For Search QA, per-dataset EM provides a breakdown of the seven-dataset average reported in the main table. SteerDistill outperforms the quantized baselines on all reported metrics. On Search QA, this advantage holds for both in-domain datasets (NQ and HotpotQA) and all five out-of-domain datasets.

C.3 Inference efficiency

For Qwen3-8B on τ2\tau^{2}-Bench, we supplement the main analysis with W2A16 and W4A8 results and detailed trajectory statistics under W4A16. Token counts, interaction steps, and tool calls are averaged over each method’s own successful tasks, so the averages cover different task subsets.

SteerDistill achieves higher Pass@1 with fewer output tokens per successful task than the quantized baselines under W2A16 and W4A8 (Figure 4), consistent with the W4A16 results in Figure 3. The detailed W4A16 statistics in Table 7 show that SteerDistill’s successful trajectories also use fewer input tokens and involve fewer interaction steps and tool calls than those of the quantized baselines.

Appendix D Additional case studies

D.1 Inference cases

We compare all seven methods on three task segments to illustrate how overlooked task requirements lead to behavioral divergence. In the train and watchlist tasks, some agents act before obtaining the missing route or company name, requesting tickets for an assumed route or removing a stock the user has not identified (Figures 5 and 7). The file-writing task is fully specified, yet some agents leave files empty or write the requested contents to the wrong files (Figure 6).

D.2 Training cases

The training cases show how teacher steering helps the student correct a failed decision from the pre-error history and state. In the file-writing and directory-navigation cases, the guidance makes an unmet prerequisite explicit: create the file before writing or enter the workspace before reading (Figures 8 and 11; see also Figure 1). In the tool-list and card-control cases, the guidance clarifies which tools and parameters to use. The student calls the advertised tool names without their list numbers or sets the flag that enforces the country restriction (Figures 9 and 10).

In the file-writing and tool-list cases, local verification checks the result of the corrected action: the newly created empty file or the unlocked doors match the reference state (Figures 8 and 9). The student then continues without the steering prompt, writing the requested sentence or turning on the headlights.

D.3 Steering prompt comparison

The ticket-creation case complements Q3 by showing how prompt format and source affect the guidance the student receives (Tables 2 and 12). Although the trading session is already authenticated, creating a ticket requires a separate login. Structured prompts from both the teacher and the student identify this prerequisite, and both continuations create the ticket after login. The free-form teacher prompt instead claims that the ticket already exists; the student logs in but stops without creating one.

The GPT-generated structured prompt also gives the correct login order and instructs the student to keep credentials out of the ticket description. The student logs in before creating the ticket but still includes the credentials in its description. This partial adherence illustrates why closed-loop teacher steering uses execution feedback to assess whether the intended behavioral correction has occurred.

D.4 Recovery cases

These cases illustrate an emergent behavior beyond the corrections explicitly targeted during training. Our trajectory revision constructs corrections from the restored pre-error history and state; at inference, the distilled student also recovers from execution errors within its ongoing rollout, without teacher guidance. In the file-writing trajectory from Figure 6, it creates the missing file after a rejected write and retries (Figure 13). In the messaging task, it successively resolves an unsupported argument and a missing login session before sending the message (Figure 14).

Appendix E Limitations

Teacher-steered trajectory revision requires successful teacher references, restoration of the pre-error history and environment state, and reliable local verification. Without a successful reference, a failed rollout is retained for distillation but receives no teacher-steered corrections. Applicability to environments without state restoration or reliable local verification remains untested. Moreover, local verification checks a revised response’s effect in the current context; it does not guarantee eventual task success or establish the correctness of every reasoning step in the response.
